headline: A bank is “money” plus “business establishment” — and that 行 is not the one that means “go”.
“Economy” is two characters borrowed from a phrase about running a state and relieving the people's suffering.
“Society” began as a gathering to honor the god of the earth, until a writer repurposed it in 1875.
“Science” was coined in Japan from Chinese parts — and it collided with “chemistry”.
Nishi Amane coined “philosophy” in 1874 — after first trying a spelling that copies the Greek.
Fireworks are “flower fire”, and the fire voices to び on the way in.
A lover is a “love person” — with the person voiced to びと.
“Pure red” — a prefix that means “true”, glued to あか.
The voicing landed one syllable late: not てづたう, but てつだう.
A room was once a “separate house” — へ plus や.
けさ is “this morning” — but the 今 in it is a stand-in for an older “this”.
A stamp borrows its two characters from “ticket” and “commercial paper”.
Cherry blossoms may be named for what they do: bloom in bursts.
A can is probably a Dutch kan in a borrowed kanji — but Chinese is the other candidate.
かぜ is just the word for “wind” — the 邪 is along for the spelling.
Beer came in through Dutch, long before English.
A button is a Portuguese word, first written down in 1651.
ガラス is Dutch, and its English cousin has its own katakana word.
A glass tumbler with two possible parents, Dutch and Portuguese.
Curry reached Japan from English, but the word starts in Tamil.
Trousers are an “underskirt”: ズボン comes from French jupon.
A “white shirt” lost its colour: ワイシャツ is a clipped ホワイトシャツ.
A mansion that shrank into an apartment: the word was meant to sound luxurious.
Often called “fake English”, サラリーマン may be real English with a letter dropped.
めがね was “eye metal” first; the kanji came from Chinese later.
The kanji say “soil” and “produce”; the likely origin is a shrine's “small box”.
いなか began as “winaka”, and its kanji came from a Chinese word.
Brothers have two readings, and they come from two waves of Chinese.
Soy sauce is “thick paste + oil”, and its sound has smoothed from /ɕauju/ to /ɕoːju/.
Buckwheat noodles carry a word whose root may be a “corner” — or a “feather”.
